segments.title: Master James's Savoyard building world
segments.body: James's influence is easier to see in castles than in the surviving record of his life. He came from the Savoy area spanning modern Switzerland, northern Italy, and southern France, where his professional and family circle worked on cathedrals and castles. Lausanne's cathedral and the wider building network reveal the architectural world in which he learned his craft. The works and workshops around him supply useful context while many details of his early life remain uncertain.

evidence.note: James's broad influence as a castle builder emerged from a Savoyard family and workshop setting connected with Lausanne.

segments.summary: The opening places Master James of St George in a Savoyard architectural world that shaped major western European castles before his Welsh work.

segments.title: What the sources cannot prove about James
segments.body: The sources do not support a simple account of James's life. Jean or John Cotereel may have been his father, his apprenticeship master, or one of two related men whom later accounts combined. Edward may also have learned of James through his mother's Savoyard relatives and retainers, so their 1273 encounter need not have been the first connection. One English-language secondary work treats John and Jean as the same person because their dates and architectural styles agree, though they may instead have been brothers. Translation can blur names and relationships, while the absence of a pension for James's wife after his death provides an inference rather than firm biographical proof. The castles remain highly visible, but the builder's life has to be reconstructed from scattered records.

evidence.note: John or Jean Cotereel may have been James's father, his master, or two separate relatives later combined in the record.
Edward's Savoyard family ties may explain his link to James, but missing family records and the pension evidence leave it unclear whether John and Jean Cotereel were one person or separate relatives.

segments.summary: Scattered records leave James's father, apprenticeship, wife, and even translated names hard to pin down.

segments.title: Vitruvius and master-mason expertise
segments.body: James's reputation as one of medieval Europe's greatest architects raises the question of what a royal castle builder needed to know. His expertise joined familiarity with Vitruvius, the surviving Roman books on architecture, with the practical standing of a master mason. Learned design principles and workshop experience reinforced one another. That combination helps explain why a king planning unusually demanding fortifications would regard James's technical competence as a strategic asset.

evidence.note: James combined the learned architecture of Vitruvius with the practical expertise of a master mason.

segments.summary: James's reputation rests on a combination of learned architectural principles and practical command of medieval masonry.

segments.title: Edward I spots a Savoy castle builder
segments.body: The lecture follows Edward's return from crusade in 1273 and his dynastic meeting with Philip I, Count of Savoy. Philip was Edward's great-nephew and needed to pay homage, so the visit joined family ties with feudal obligation. Philip also had several castles under construction, with James already running or heavily involved in the work. Edward could therefore judge the builder through visible engineering performance. The contact did not produce an immediate move because Edward had no Welsh castle program underway, but James appears in Wales in 1278 as a works coordinator. The sequence shows recruitment through dynastic networks, political obligation, patronage, and demonstrated technical ability.

evidence.note: Philip of Savoy's homage and family relationship brought Edward into contact with several Savoy castle projects involving James.
After Edward had seen James's work in Savoy, James appeared in Wales in 1278 as a building coordinator.

segments.summary: Edward I's visit to receive Philip of Savoy's homage also exposed him to the castle work that would bring James to Wales.

segments.title: Master of construction in Wales
segments.body: James's promotion turned a skilled builder into a powerful royal officer. Edward, frustrated with the pace of construction, made him master of the king's works in Wales. A wage of three shillings a day and direct control over Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech, and eventually Beaumaris show the scale of that authority. French and Latin versions of James's name and title explain why the same official appears differently across documents. The appointment helps explain how the Ring of Iron operated as an integrated royal building program rather than a set of isolated local projects.

evidence.note: Edward's impatience with construction speed led him to make James master of the king's works in Wales.
James held full control over work at Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech, and Beaumaris, while French and Latin records rendered his name differently.

segments.summary: James's promotion gave him direct royal authority over the great Welsh castle works at Conwy, Caernarfon, Harlech, and Beaumaris.

segments.title: Castle builder as royal military officer
segments.body: James's career extended beyond technical design. He served as constable of Harlech from 1290 to 1293, making him the king's representative inside a fortress he had helped shape. The office implied trust in his ability to manage and, if necessary, fight the castle. Edward summoned him to Scotland in 1298, and the record places him at Stirling during the 1304 siege. Design, garrison responsibility, and campaign fortification were connected parts of his royal service.

evidence.note: James's appointment as constable of Harlech showed that he was trusted to command and defend a castle he had helped design.
Edward called James to Scotland, where he worked at Stirling during the siege of 1304.

segments.summary: James designed castles, held Harlech as constable, and supported Edward's Scottish campaigns.

segments.title: Sea-supplied castles as occupation deterrence
segments.body: James's work belongs in a sea-power account of the Ring of Iron because Edward's castles depended on water access for security, supply, and reinforcements. A weak fortress might fall before that maritime lifeline could have any effect, so walls, siting, and the use of terrain formed part of the same logistical system. The castles served as engines of occupation and deterrence. Fortress architecture, naval logistics, and political control all had to work together.

evidence.note: The transcript calls the castles engines of deterrence and occupation dependent on water access for security and supply.
Edward needed a master architect who could make each castle as strong as possible while adapting it to the ground.

segments.summary: The central sea-power argument ties James's castle design to water access, reinforcement, and the deterrent machinery of occupation.

segments.title: Reading castle construction at Beaumaris
segments.body: Beaumaris Castle offers a practical way to read construction evidence on site. The attractive image shown on screen is highly idealized, while displays inside the castle explain the tools and methods used to build it. That contrast separates the picturesque finished fortress from the labor and technique that produced it. James's reputation becomes easier to understand when set beside the material practice of medieval castle building.

evidence.note: An idealized image of Beaumaris contrasts with the castle's displays on the tools and methods used to build it.

segments.summary: Beaumaris connects idealized castle imagery with the tools and building methods behind the masonry.

segments.title: Which Ring of Iron castles James controlled
segments.body: The castle-by-castle survey avoids crediting every Welsh fortress to one famous architect. Flint, Rhuddlan, Hawarden, Harlech, Caernarfon, Conwy, and Beaumaris form the core of the work attributed to James. Denbigh may reflect his influence because it lay within his operating area, while Aberystwyth and Builth receive more cautious treatment. Good deputies extended his reach, but even a powerful master of works could not supervise every site directly. The distinction separates broad architectural influence from documented personal control.

evidence.note: The transcript reviews which castles James controlled or influenced and notes limits on what one person could oversee.

segments.summary: A castle-by-castle survey separates sites James clearly controlled from places where his involvement remains likely, limited, or uncertain.

segments.title: Flint, Rhuddlan, and Hawarden built for speed
segments.body: Flint was James's primary early responsibility, and he also oversaw work at Rhuddlan and Hawarden. These castles belonged to the first group completed and secured quickly. James continued to move among the sites rather than treating each commission as an isolated project. Speed mattered to Edward I, so reliable delivery gave the king a practical reason to expand James's authority. Construction performance led directly to greater royal confidence and promotion.

evidence.note: The transcript returns to Flint, Rhuddlan, and Hawarden as early fast-built castles and links that speed to Edward's preference.

segments.summary: The fast construction of James's first three Welsh responsibilities helps explain why Edward entrusted him with a wider castle program.
